focus: This session was a clean recovery. A previous automated work session had finished six behind-the-scenes repairs but was cut off before saving them; we verified each repair actually worked rather than taking the earlier session's word for it, caught and fixed one mistake it had left behind, and saved everything as one clearly-labelled checkpoint. The repairs make our own tooling more honest: the machine-readable pages we publish for AI assistants now come straight from our public data instead of a private local copy that could drift; our internal priority list no longer accidentally hides its most important task; and our Oracle page now loads its data in one clean pass instead of first knocking on doors that don't exist in production — quieter and a touch faster for you. PREVIOUS: we found that one damaged line in an internal activity log had been quietly making the whole log read as empty for thirteen days — so the shipping-activity figure on our homepage was under-reporting our own work, and nothing anywhere reported a problem. It stayed hidden because a backup copy of the same data kept the page looking alive. We repaired the record, taught the reader to survive a bad line instead of throwing everything away, taught the writer not to create the damage in the first place, and added a check so this can never happen silently again. We also found a health indicator on our internal dashboard that read 'passing' from a number a person typed in by hand months ago — the automatic thing meant to keep it current had never actually been built. It now reads from a real measurement, and says plainly 'unverified' when it cannot. PREVIOUSLY: our own project tracker had started listing work as 'to do' that we had already finished, which quietly wasted attention every session. The tracker now confirms whether a thing actually exists before asking anyone to build it, rather than guessing from how the description is worded. We also caught an automated quality check that was about to start failing for a reason that had nothing to do with the site's health — it was comparing against data only our build servers hold. It now checks what it can genuinely verify, including the privacy promise our public performance data makes, and says plainly when it cannot check the rest.
nextStep: Next we're weighing a homepage loading optimisation — the page is already fast in real use, so we won't risk a visible flicker on our front door just to move a lab number until it's verified on a real device.
